paragraphs: The moment the people is lawfully assembled as a sovereign body, the government loses all jurisdiction and the executive power is suspended. The person of the humblest citizen becomes as sacred and inviolable as that of the first magistrate, for where the person represented is present, there are no representatives. Most of the tumults in the Roman comitia came from ignorance or neglect of this rule. In those assemblies the consuls were merely the presidents of the people, the tribunes were mere speakers,[1] and the senate was nothing at all.

These intervals of suspension, during which the prince recognizes, or ought to recognize, an actual superior, have always alarmed him; and these assemblies of the people, which are the shield of the body politic and the curb on the government, have at all times been the horror of rulers, who therefore never spare effort, objections, difficulties and promises to keep the citizens from holding them. When the citizens are greedy, cowardly and fainthearted, and love ease more than liberty, they do not hold out long against the redoubled efforts of the government; and so, as the resisting force grows without end, the sovereign authority finally disappears, and most cities fall and perish before their time.
But between the sovereign authority and arbitrary government there sometimes comes an intermediate power, of which something must be said.
Parliament. These functions were so similar that they would have set the consuls and the tribunes against each other, even if all jurisdiction had been suspended.
